title: Properties of softmax cross-entropy
prompt: Which statements about the cross-entropy loss with softmax are correct?

options.text: It stays strictly positive for any finite scores.
options.explanation: With finite scores the softmax probability of the correct class is strictly below 1 (the other classes keep some mass), so $-\log p_y > 0$.

options.text: Minimizing it is equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood of the correct class.
options.explanation: The loss is $-\log p_y$, the negative log-likelihood of the label, so minimizing the loss maximizes $\log p_y$.

options.text: It reaches exactly zero as soon as the sample is classified correctly.
options.explanation: Correct classification only needs the correct class to have the largest score. The loss is zero only if $p_y = 1$, which needs an infinite margin; a correct but unconfident prediction still has positive loss.

options.text: It equals the negative logarithm of the probability assigned to the correct class.
options.explanation: For a one-hot target the sum $-\sum_k t_k \log p_k$ keeps only the correct-class term, which is $-\log p_y$.

hints: Write the loss for a one-hot target and see which terms of the sum survive.
When is $-\log p$ exactly zero?
explanation: With a one-hot target the cross-entropy collapses to $L = -\log p_y$, where $p_y$ is the softmax probability of the correct class. This is the negative log-likelihood, so minimizing it is maximum-likelihood training. Because softmax never outputs exactly 1 for finite scores, the loss is always positive and keeps pushing the correct score further above the others, even for already correctly classified samples.

title: Components of Mitchell's definition of learning
prompt: According to Mitchell's definition of machine learning ("A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E"), which components appear in the definition?

options.text: A task T
options.explanation: The definition is about performance on a class of tasks T, such as classifying images.

options.text: A regularization weight lambda
options.explanation: A regularization weight is a hyperparameter of some training methods, not part of the definition. The definition is independent of how learning is implemented.

options.text: An experience E
options.explanation: Learning means improving with experience E, for example the training data.

options.text: A network architecture A
options.explanation: Mitchell's definition does not mention any model family or architecture; it applies to neural networks, decision trees and others alike.

options.text: A performance measure P
options.explanation: Improvement must be measured, for example by accuracy or loss, so a performance measure P is needed.

hints: The definition has three letters.
Does the definition say anything about how the program is built?
explanation: Mitchell defines learning by three ingredients: a task T, a performance measure P and an experience E, such that performance on T measured by P improves with E. It is deliberately independent of the model, architecture or training details, so hyperparameters like a regularization weight or an architecture do not appear.

title: Size of the ILSVRC dataset
prompt: Roughly how many images does the 1,000-class ILSVRC challenge dataset contain?

options.text: About 60,000
options.explanation: 60,000 is the size of CIFAR-10 (50,000 training + 10,000 test images of 32x32 pixels), a much smaller dataset.

options.text: About 15 million
options.explanation: Roughly 14-15 million is the size of the full ImageNet collection with about 21,000 categories, not of the 1,000-class ILSVRC subset.

options.text: About 5.85 billion
options.explanation: This is the order of magnitude of web-scale datasets such as LAION-5B, far beyond ILSVRC.

options.text: About 1.4 million
options.explanation: ILSVRC has about 1.28 million training images plus 50,000 validation and 100,000 test images, i.e. roughly 1.4 million in total.

hints: Think of the 1,000-class challenge subset, not of the whole ImageNet collection.
CIFAR-10 has 60,000 images; ILSVRC is more than 20 times larger.
explanation: The ILSVRC (ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge) uses 1,000 classes and roughly 1.4 million images in total, about 1.28 million of them for training. Do not confuse it with CIFAR-10 (60,000 small images), the full ImageNet (about 14-15 million images, ~21k classes) or billion-scale web datasets.

title: Measures against overfitting
prompt: Which measures typically reduce overfitting?

options.text: Selecting a lower model complexity based on validation error.
options.explanation: A simpler model has less capacity to fit noise, and choosing the complexity on held-out validation error picks the point where generalization is best.

options.text: Tuning hyperparameters directly on the test set.
options.explanation: This leaks information from the test set into the model choice, so the test error becomes an optimistic estimate; it does not reduce overfitting. Hyperparameters should be tuned on a separate validation set.

options.text: Collecting more training data.
options.explanation: More samples constrain the model more tightly, so it is harder to fit noise or idiosyncrasies of a small sample.

options.text: Adding a regularization term that penalizes large coefficient magnitudes.
options.explanation: Penalties such as weight decay discourage extreme weights, which shrinks the effective complexity and smooths the learned function.

options.text: Increasing the polynomial order as much as possible.
options.explanation: Higher order means higher capacity, so the model fits the training points (and their noise) ever more closely and overfits more, not less.

hints: Overfitting means the capacity is too large relative to the data. Which options reduce capacity or increase data?
Which option contaminates the data that is supposed to measure generalization?
explanation: Overfitting is reduced by lowering effective model capacity (simpler models, regularization) or by providing more data, and by selecting these choices with a validation set. Raising capacity makes it worse, and tuning on the test set does not fight overfitting but destroys the test set as an unbiased estimate.

title: One-hot label vectors for CIFAR-10
prompt: Which statements about the one-hot encoding of a CIFAR-10 class label are correct?

options.text: The entries sum to 1.
options.explanation: Exactly one entry is 1 and all others are 0, so the sum is 1.

options.text: Exactly one entry equals 1 and all other entries equal 0.
options.explanation: This is the definition of one-hot: the entry at the index of the true class is 1.

options.text: The entries are probabilities learned by the classifier.
options.explanation: The one-hot vector is the ground-truth target, fixed by the dataset label. The probabilities learned by the classifier are the softmax outputs, which the loss compares to this target.

options.text: The vector has exactly 10 entries.
options.explanation: CIFAR-10 has 10 classes, and a one-hot vector has one entry per class.

options.text: The vector has 3,072 entries.
options.explanation: 3,072 = 32*32*3 is the number of values in a CIFAR-10 input image, not the length of the label vector, which equals the number of classes (10).

hints: A one-hot vector has one slot per class.
3,072 is the size of the input, not of the label.
explanation: A one-hot label is a length-K vector (K = 10 for CIFAR-10) with a single 1 at the true class and 0 elsewhere, so it sums to 1. It is the target distribution that the predicted softmax probabilities are compared against. Keep apart the label dimension (number of classes) and the input dimension (3,072 pixel values).

title: What is generalization?
prompt: What is generalization?

options.text: Achieving zero error on the training data.
options.explanation: Zero training error says nothing about unseen data; a model that memorizes the training set achieves it and may still generalize badly.

options.text: Increasing the number of model parameters.
options.explanation: More parameters raise capacity, which can even hurt generalization; it is a modelling choice, not the definition of generalization.

options.text: Making accurate predictions on unseen inputs.
options.explanation: Generalization is performance on new data drawn from the same distribution, which is what a deployed model is judged on.

options.text: Memorizing all training samples.
options.explanation: Memorization is the opposite of generalization: the model reproduces the training data (including noise) but fails on new inputs, which is overfitting.

hints: On which data is generalization measured?
Is a model that perfectly memorizes the training set necessarily useful?
explanation: Generalization is the ability of a model to perform well on inputs it has not seen during training. Training error, parameter count or memorization do not measure it; this is why we evaluate on held-out validation and test data.

title: Challenges of image classification
prompt: Which of the following are recognized challenges of the image classification problem?

options.text: Occlusion
options.explanation: Parts of the object may be hidden by other objects, yet it must still be recognized.

options.text: All datasets containing exactly 10 classes
options.explanation: The number of classes in a dataset is not an intrinsic challenge of the task; datasets range from 2 to thousands of classes. The real challenges concern how images of one class vary.

options.text: Illumination conditions
options.explanation: Lighting changes the pixel values drastically without changing the object's identity.

options.text: Background clutter
options.explanation: Objects can blend into a busy background, making them hard to separate from it.

options.text: Scale variation
options.explanation: The same object can appear at very different sizes in the image, changing its pixel pattern.

options.text: Viewpoint variation
options.explanation: Moving the camera changes the image of the same object, so the pixel values change entirely.

hints: Think of what can change between two photos of the same object.
Which option is a property of a dataset rather than of the images?
explanation: Image classification is hard because the pixel values change a lot when the object is moved, rotated, scaled, lit differently, partly hidden or placed in a cluttered scene (and when instances of a class look different), while the label must stay the same. A fixed dataset size or class count is a design property of a benchmark, not a challenge of the task.

title: A polynomial as a linear model
prompt: Why does the polynomial $y(x,w)=w_0+w_1 x+\dots+w_M x^M$ count as a linear model?

options.text: Its graph is always a straight line.
options.explanation: For $M \geq 2$ the graph is a curve (a parabola, cubic, ...). "Linear model" does not refer to the shape of the graph.

options.text: It is linear in the unknown parameters $w$, even though it is nonlinear in the input $x$.
options.explanation: The output is a weighted sum $\sum_j w_j x^j$ of fixed features $x^j$, so it is linear in $w$, which is all that matters for fitting.

options.text: It is linear in the input $x$.
options.explanation: Terms like $x^2$ and $x^3$ make the function nonlinear in $x$: doubling $x$ does not double the output.

options.text: It contains no powers of $x$ greater than 1.
options.explanation: It explicitly contains powers up to $x^M$. It is still a linear model because those powers are fixed features and the parameters enter linearly.

hints: Linear with respect to what: the input or the parameters you are fitting?
Treat $x, x^2, \dots, x^M$ as ready-made features.
explanation: A linear model is linear in its parameters: $y = \sum_j w_j \phi_j(x)$ with fixed basis functions $\phi_j(x) = x^j$. The curve can be strongly nonlinear in $x$, but because the parameters enter linearly, the fit reduces to linear least squares with a closed-form solution.

title: Roles of the data splits
prompt: Which statements about the training / validation / test split are correct?

options.text: The training set is used to fit the model parameters (weights).
options.explanation: The weights are optimized by minimizing the loss on the training data only.

options.text: The test set should be used only once, for the final evaluation.
options.explanation: Every look at the test set that influences a decision makes its estimate optimistic; it should be used once at the very end.

options.text: The validation set is also called the development (dev) set.
options.explanation: Both names refer to the held-out set used during development to compare models and settings.

options.text: The validation set is used to choose hyperparameters such as the model complexity.
options.explanation: Hyperparameters cannot be fitted on the training loss (it favours the most complex model), so they are selected by the error on held-out validation data.

options.text: The test set should be evaluated every epoch to guide training decisions.
options.explanation: Using the test set to guide decisions (early stopping, tuning) turns it into a validation set and biases the final estimate. Use the validation set for monitoring.

hints: Which set may influence decisions and which one must stay untouched?
Weights and hyperparameters are chosen on different sets.
explanation: Training data fits the weights, validation (dev) data selects hyperparameters and models, and the test set is kept untouched until a single final evaluation so that it gives an unbiased estimate of generalization. Once test results influence decisions, the test set is no longer independent.

title: Data points versus number of parameters
prompt: Which statements about the amount of data relative to the number of model parameters are correct?

options.text: Classical ML works best when parameters outnumber data points.
options.explanation: Classical models with more parameters than data points can fit the training set perfectly and overfit badly; the usual advice is the opposite, several data points per parameter.

options.text: Both classical ML and deep learning strictly require more data points than parameters.
options.explanation: The requirement is not strict for deep learning: modern networks routinely have far more parameters than training samples and still generalize well, helped by regularization, data augmentation and the implicit bias of SGD.

options.text: Deep learning never works when the parameters outnumber the samples.
options.explanation: "Never" is false: heavily over-parameterized networks are the norm in deep learning and often achieve excellent test performance.

options.text: Classical ML suggests 5 to 10 times more data points than parameters, yet deep networks often achieve great results with more parameters than training samples.
options.explanation: This is the rule of thumb for classical models, and deep learning is the well-known exception that works in the over-parameterized regime.

hints: Think of a polynomial with as many coefficients as data points, then of a modern CNN with millions of weights.
Is the rule of thumb for classical ML a strict law for every model family?
explanation: For classical models a common rule of thumb is 5 to 10 data points per parameter, because with too few points the model memorizes noise. Deep networks break this intuition: they are usually over-parameterized and still generalize, thanks to regularization, augmentation, early stopping and the implicit bias of gradient-based training. Statements that turn the rule into a strict requirement (or say the opposite) are therefore wrong.

title: Properties of softmax
prompt: Which properties of the softmax function $p_i = e^{s_i} / \sum_j e^{s_j}$ are correct?

options.text: Multiplying all scores by 2 leaves the outputs unchanged.
options.explanation: Softmax is invariant to additive shifts, not to scaling. Doubling the scores sharpens the distribution: for scores (1, 0) the output changes from about (0.73, 0.27) to about (0.88, 0.12).

options.text: The ranking of the scores is preserved in the output probabilities.
options.explanation: The exponential is strictly increasing and the denominator is shared, so a larger score always gives a larger probability.

options.text: The outputs sum to 1.
options.explanation: Each output is $e^{s_i}$ divided by the sum of all $e^{s_j}$, so they add up to exactly 1.

options.text: Adding the same constant to every input score leaves the outputs unchanged.
options.explanation: $e^{s_i + c} / \sum_j e^{s_j + c} = e^c e^{s_i} / (e^c \sum_j e^{s_j})$, and the factor $e^c$ cancels. This is why one subtracts the maximum score for numerical stability.

options.text: All outputs are strictly between 0 and 1.
options.explanation: Every $e^{s_i}$ is positive, so each output is above 0, and with at least two classes the other terms keep each output below 1.

hints: Compare softmax of (1, 0) with softmax of (2, 0) and with softmax of (2, 1).
Factor out a constant from numerator and denominator.
explanation: Softmax maps scores to a probability distribution with strictly positive entries summing to 1, and it preserves the order of the scores because the exponential is increasing. It is invariant to adding a constant to all scores (the factor cancels), which allows subtracting the maximum for numerical stability, but not to scaling the scores, which changes how peaked the distribution is.

title: Chairs that look nothing alike
prompt: A class contains objects that look very different from one another (for example, many different kinds of chairs). Which challenge does this illustrate?

options.text: Occlusion
options.explanation: Occlusion means that parts of an object are hidden by something else in the image, not that instances of the class differ.

options.text: Viewpoint variation
options.explanation: Viewpoint variation concerns the same object seen from different camera positions, not different objects of one class.

options.text: Background clutter
options.explanation: Clutter is about the surroundings of the object hiding or resembling it, not about the diversity of objects inside the class.

options.text: Intra-class variation
options.explanation: Different instances of the same class (armchairs, stools, office chairs) can differ strongly in shape, colour and material while sharing one label.

hints: The variation here is among different objects, not among different photos of one object.
Which challenge is named after variation inside a class?
explanation: Intra-class variation is the challenge that instances of a single category can look very different, so the classifier must learn what they share rather than how any single instance looks. The other options describe changes in how one object is imaged (viewpoint, occlusion, clutter).

title: Which learning paradigm uses partial labels?
prompt: Which statements best describe semi-supervised learning?

options.text: Labels are available for only a subset of the data; the rest of the data is unlabeled.
options.explanation: Semi-supervised learning combines a small labeled set with a large unlabeled set.

options.text: All data points come with labels.
options.explanation: That is the fully supervised setting. Semi-supervised learning is motivated by labels being expensive, so only some samples have them.

options.text: Labels are derived automatically from the data itself.
options.explanation: That describes self-supervised learning, where a pretext task creates labels from the data. In semi-supervised learning real labels exist for a subset.

options.text: The model receives rewards instead of labels.
options.explanation: Rewards are the feedback of reinforcement learning, not of semi-supervised learning.

hints: Place each option into supervised, self-supervised or reinforcement learning first.
The prefix 'semi' hints at something partial.
explanation: Semi-supervised learning sits between supervised and unsupervised learning: only a subset of the samples is labeled and the unlabeled rest is used to improve the model. Fully labeled data is supervised, labels generated from the data itself is self-supervised, and reward signals indicate reinforcement learning.

title: Output of image segmentation
prompt: What are the outputs of image segmentation for an image with C classes?

options.text: A single class label for the entire image.
options.explanation: That is the output of image classification. Segmentation labels every pixel individually.

options.text: An image of class labels in which every pixel has a value in the range [0, C-1].
options.explanation: Semantic segmentation assigns each pixel one of the C classes, giving a label map with the same spatial size as the input.

options.text: One probability value for the whole image.
options.explanation: A single image-level probability corresponds to a binary image-level decision, not to a per-pixel prediction for C classes.

options.text: A list of bounding boxes and their labels.
options.explanation: Boxes with labels are the output of object detection. Segmentation gives dense per-pixel labels instead of boxes.

hints: Segmentation is a dense prediction task.
What is the spatial size of the output compared to the input?
explanation: Segmentation predicts a class for every pixel, so its output is a label map of the same height and width as the input with values in [0, C-1]. Classification gives one label per image and detection gives a list of boxes with labels.

title: AI, ML and DL: how they nest
prompt: Which statements about the AI / ML / DL hierarchy are correct?

options.text: Machine learning is a subfield of artificial intelligence.
options.explanation: AI is the broad goal of intelligent machines, and machine learning is the part of it that learns from data.

options.text: Every deep learning method is also a machine learning method.
options.explanation: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning, so any deep learning method is by definition a machine learning method.

options.text: Every machine learning method is a deep learning method.
options.explanation: The inclusion goes the other way. Linear regression, SVMs and decision trees are machine learning but not deep learning, since they do not use deep neural networks.

options.text: Deep learning is a subfield of machine learning.
options.explanation: Deep learning is the part of machine learning that learns hierarchical representations with multi-layer neural networks.

options.text: Artificial intelligence is a subfield of machine learning.
options.explanation: This reverses the nesting. AI is the largest field; some AI systems, such as hand-written rule-based systems, do not learn at all.

hints: Draw three nested circles.
Name a machine learning method that is not a deep network.
explanation: The fields nest as deep learning inside machine learning inside artificial intelligence. Every statement that goes from the inner to the outer field is true; the reverse direction is false.

title: Building one-hot vectors in PyTorch
prompt: $y$ holds integer class indices with shape $(N,)$ for a $K$-class problem. Which snippet creates float one-hot vectors of shape $(N,K)$ without materializing a $K\times K$ identity matrix?

options.text: `F.one_hot(y, num_classes=K).float()`
options.explanation: `F.one_hot` builds the $(N, K)$ integer tensor directly, and `num_classes=K` fixes the width; `.float()` converts it to float.

options.text: `torch.zeros(K).scatter_(0, y, 1.0)`
options.explanation: This creates a single vector of shape $(K,)$ with ones at all indices in `y`, not one row per sample, so the shape is wrong.

options.text: `torch.eye(K)[y]`
options.explanation: The result has the right shape $(N, K)$, but it first builds the full $K\times K$ identity matrix and then indexes its rows, which is exactly what the question excludes.

options.text: `F.one_hot(y).float()`
options.explanation: Without `num_classes` the width is inferred as `y.max() + 1`, which is smaller than $K$ whenever the largest class does not occur in `y`, so the shape is not guaranteed to be $(N, K)$.

hints: Check the output shape of each snippet first, then the memory behaviour.
What does `F.one_hot` do when `num_classes` is omitted?
explanation: Only one snippet is correct on both counts: it has the guaranteed shape $(N, K)$ and does not build a $K\times K$ matrix. Always pass `num_classes` to `F.one_hot` so the width does not depend on which classes happen to appear in the batch.

title: Recognizing overfitting
prompt: Which observations indicate overfitting?

options.text: High error on both the training set and the test set.
options.explanation: If the model is poor even on the training data, it is underfitting (too little capacity or too little training), not overfitting.

options.text: A large gap between training error and test error.
options.explanation: The model has fitted the training data much better than it performs on new data, which is the definition of overfitting.

options.text: In polynomial fitting, coefficients growing to very large magnitudes as the order $M$ increases.
options.explanation: To pass through noisy points exactly, high-order polynomials need huge, oscillating coefficients that cancel each other, a typical symptom of overfitting.

options.text: Low error on the training set but high error on the test set.
options.explanation: This is the classic overfitting signature: the training data is memorized but the model does not generalize.

hints: Overfitting is about the difference between performance on seen and unseen data.
What would a model look like that has high error even on the training set?
explanation: Overfitting shows up as low training error combined with high test error, i.e. a large generalization gap; in polynomial regression it also appears as exploding coefficients. High error on both sets means underfitting, which has a different cure (more capacity rather than more regularization).

title: Visualizing a linear classifier
prompt: When the 'templates' of a CIFAR-10 linear classifier $s = Wx + b$ with $W \in \mathbb{R}^{10\times 3072}$ are visualized as images, what exactly are shown?

options.text: The rows of $W$, reshaped to image dimensions, one template per class.
options.explanation: The score of class $k$ is $w_k \cdot x + b_k$, where $w_k$ is row $k$ of $W$. This row has 3072 values and reshapes to a 32x32x3 image, the template that the input is matched against.

options.text: The class probability vectors produced by the classifier.
options.explanation: Probabilities are outputs for a given input with only 10 entries each; they are not images and are not parameters of the model.

options.text: The training images that received the highest scores.
options.explanation: Templates are learned weights, not training images. They are blurry averages of what the class looks like, not particular samples.

options.text: The columns of $W$, one per input pixel.
options.explanation: A column of $W$ has only 10 entries (one weight per class for a single input value) and cannot be reshaped to an image. Templates are rows, with one entry per input value.

hints: Which dimension of $W$ has the size of an image, 3072?
Which weights are multiplied with $x$ to produce one class score?
explanation: Each row of $W$ holds the weights that produce one class score by a dot product with the flattened image, so a row reshaped to 32x32x3 is that class's template. Columns correspond to input pixels, with one weight per class, and are not templates.

title: Flattening while keeping the batch dimension
prompt: A tensor `x` has shape (N, C, H, W). Which lines flatten it to shape (N, C*H*W), preserving the batch dimension?

options.text: `x.reshape(x.shape[0], -1)`
options.explanation: The first dimension stays N and -1 lets PyTorch infer C*H*W, so the result is (N, C*H*W).

options.text: `x.view(x.size(0), -1)`
options.explanation: Same as reshape with the batch size kept explicitly; view works here because a freshly created contiguous tensor can be viewed with any compatible shape.

options.text: `x.flatten(start_dim=1)`
options.explanation: Flattening starts at dimension 1, so dimension 0 (the batch) is untouched and C, H, W are merged into C*H*W.

options.text: `x.view(-1)`
options.explanation: This flattens everything, including the batch dimension, into a 1-D tensor of shape (N*C*H*W,). Samples are no longer separate rows.

options.text: `x.squeeze()`
options.explanation: squeeze only removes dimensions of size 1; it does not merge C, H and W, so for typical shapes the tensor stays 4-D.

hints: Which dimension must stay separate?
What does -1 mean in reshape/view, and does squeeze merge dimensions?
explanation: To feed feature maps into a linear layer you need one row per sample, i.e. keep dimension 0 and merge all others. reshape/view with (N, -1) and flatten(start_dim=1) do this. view(-1) merges the batch too, and squeeze merely drops size-1 dimensions.

title: LeCun's cake analogy
prompt: In LeCun's cake analogy (LeCake), which statements are correct?

options.text: Pure reinforcement learning is the cherry on top, with only a few bits for some samples.
options.explanation: Rewards give very little information per sample, so reinforcement learning is the small cherry on the cake.

options.text: Self-supervised learning is the main body of the cake, with millions of bits of feedback per sample.
options.explanation: Predicting parts of the data from other parts supplies a huge amount of supervision per sample, making it the bulk of the cake.

options.text: Reinforcement learning provides the richest feedback signal per sample.
options.explanation: It is the opposite: reinforcement learning has the sparsest feedback (a few bits, a scalar reward), the cherry on top. The richest signal is in self-supervised learning.

options.text: Supervised learning is the icing, with roughly 10 to 10,000 bits per sample.
options.explanation: A label or a category/vector per sample carries moderate information, so supervised learning is the icing, between the cake and the cherry.

hints: The cake is ordered by amount of feedback per sample.
Which paradigm gets only a scalar reward?
explanation: In LeCun's analogy the amount of information per sample orders the paradigms: self-supervised learning (millions of bits) is the cake, supervised learning (10 to 10,000 bits) is the icing, and reinforcement learning (a few bits) is the cherry. The point is that most of what a system learns should come from self-supervised prediction.

title: Shift invariance of softmax and positive cross-entropy
prompt: Explain why softmax outputs do not change when the same constant is added to all scores, and why the cross-entropy loss of a correctly classified sample is nevertheless never exactly zero.
model_answer: Adding a constant $c$ multiplies every $e^{s_i}$ by $e^c$, and the same factor appears in the denominator, so it cancels and the probabilities are unchanged (this is why subtracting the maximum score is a safe trick for numerical stability). Cross-entropy with a one-hot target is $-\log p_y$. Because every exponential is positive, $p_y < 1$ for finite scores, so the loss is strictly positive. A sample can be classified correctly, meaning that $p_y$ is the largest probability, while $p_y$ is still well below 1, so the loss keeps pushing the correct score further above the rest.
key_points: The constant factor $e^c$ cancels between numerator and denominator.
Subtracting the maximum score is used for numerical stability without changing the output.
Cross-entropy reduces to $-\log p_y$ for a one-hot target.
$p_y < 1$ for finite scores, hence the loss is strictly positive; correct classification only requires the largest score.
hints: Write out the softmax of $s_i + c$.
What value would $p_y$ need to have for $-\log p_y = 0$?
explanation: The shift invariance follows directly from factoring $e^c$ out of every term, and it matters in practice because large scores would overflow the exponential. The loss is positive because it measures confidence, not only correctness. A common half-answer says that the loss is zero once the argmax is right; that confuses the accuracy criterion with the likelihood criterion that the loss actually optimizes.

title: High-order polynomials and the role of the validation set
prompt: You fit a polynomial of order $M$ to a small noisy dataset. Explain what happens to the training and test error and to the coefficients as $M$ grows very large, and why a separate validation set (rather than the test set) should be used to pick $M$.
model_answer: As $M$ grows, the polynomial gains capacity and can pass through the training points almost exactly, so the training error keeps falling toward zero. It also fits the noise, so the test error eventually rises, and the coefficients become very large with opposite signs to produce the wiggles. The order $M$ is a hyperparameter and cannot be chosen on the training error, which always favours the largest $M$. It must be chosen on held-out data, and if the test set were used, the final test error would be an optimistically biased estimate. A validation set keeps the test set for one final unbiased evaluation. Regularization or more data counteract the overfitting.
key_points: Training error keeps decreasing with $M$ while test error eventually increases (overfitting).
Coefficients grow to large magnitudes because the high-order fit chases the noise.
$M$ is a hyperparameter selected on validation data, not on training error.
Using the test set for selection biases the final estimate; it should be used once at the end.
Regularization or more training data reduce the overfitting.
hints: Which error can always be lowered by adding capacity?
What happens to the independence of the test set if you make choices based on it?
explanation: The answer connects four ideas: capacity versus noise, the signature of overfitting (a training/test gap and exploding coefficients), hyperparameter selection on a validation set, and keeping the test set untouched. Typical mistakes are to say that the training error also increases for large $M$ (it does not, it goes down), or to select $M$ on the test set because it is the data that measures generalization, which makes the reported test error biased.

title: Defining supervised learning
prompt: Which statements best describe supervised learning? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Generate labels from the data itself and predict parts of the input from other parts
options.explanation: This describes self-supervised learning: the labels are derived automatically from the data (e.g. a masked word or a future frame). Supervised learning relies on labels that come from outside the data, usually from human annotators.

options.text: An agent interacts with an environment to maximize a reward
options.explanation: This is reinforcement learning, where the signal is a scalar reward obtained from interaction rather than a correct target for every input.

options.text: Find structure or patterns in data without any labels
options.explanation: This is unsupervised learning (clustering, dimensionality reduction, ...). Supervised learning always has labels; their absence is exactly what separates the two.

options.text: Given data together with labels, learn a general rule that maps inputs to labels
options.explanation: This is the definition: training pairs (input, label) are used to learn a function that should also predict the label of new, unseen inputs.

explanation: The learning paradigms differ in where the training signal comes from. Supervised learning gets an explicit label for each input and learns an input-to-label mapping that generalizes; unsupervised learning has no labels; self-supervised learning builds its own labels from the data; reinforcement learning uses rewards. Ask yourself 'what is the supervision signal?' to tell them apart.

title: Rank of an image-batch tensor
prompt: A batch of $N$ RGB images (each with a height, a width and 3 colour channels) is stored as a single tensor. What is the rank of this tensor, i.e. how many axes does it have?
hints: List the kinds of index you need to address a single number in the batch: which sample, which colour, and then which pixel.
The batch itself counts as an axis.
explanation:
To pick out one number you need four indices: the sample in the batch, the channel (R, G or B), the row and the column. The shape is $(N, 3, H, W)$ in PyTorch (or $(N, H, W, 3)$ in channels-last layouts), so the rank is 4 either way.

Typical wrong answers: 3 forgets the batch axis (that is the rank of a single image); 5 would be needed for something like a video batch with an extra time axis; 2 corresponds to a matrix such as the flattened batch of shape $(N, 3HW)$, which is no longer an image tensor.

title: Parameters of a linear CIFAR-10 classifier
prompt: A linear classifier for CIFAR-10 computes the 10 class scores as $s = Wx + b$ from a flattened 32x32x3 image $x$ (3,072 values). How many trainable parameters do $W$ and $b$ have together?
hints: What shape must $W$ have to turn a vector of 3,072 values into 10 scores?
There is one bias per class.
explanation:
$W \in \mathbb{R}^{10\times 3072}$ has $10\cdot 3072 = 30{,}720$ weights, and $b \in \mathbb{R}^{10}$ adds 10 biases, so the total is $30{,}720 + 10 = 30{,}730$.

The tempting wrong answers: 3,072 is just the input dimension (or the weights of a single class); 30,720 forgets the biases; 3,082 counts only one weight row (3,072) plus the 10 biases, i.e. it forgets that every one of the 10 classes has its own weight vector.

title: Facts about ImageNet and ILSVRC
prompt: Which statements about ImageNet and the ILSVRC challenge are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The full ImageNet database contains roughly 22,000 categories and about 15 million images
options.explanation: The complete ImageNet collection has on the order of 22,000 categories (WordNet synsets) and roughly 14-15 million labelled images.

options.text: The ILSVRC classification challenge uses 1,000 object classes
options.explanation: ILSVRC uses a curated subset of 1,000 classes with about 1.2 million training images; this is the 'ImageNet' most papers report results on.

options.text: The ILSVRC classification challenge uses exactly 10 classes
options.explanation: Ten classes is the size of CIFAR-10, not ILSVRC. Mixing the two up is common because both are 'image classification benchmarks'.

options.text: The annotation process was crowdsourced
options.explanation: Candidate images were collected from the web and verified by many workers on a crowdsourcing platform (Amazon Mechanical Turk), which is what made labelling millions of images feasible.

options.text: ImageNet's categories are based on the WordNet database
options.explanation: Each ImageNet category corresponds to a WordNet synset (a set of synonyms for a concept), which gives the classes a noun hierarchy.

explanation: ImageNet is a very large, hierarchically organized image database whose categories come from WordNet and whose labels were collected by crowdsourcing. The yearly ILSVRC challenge uses a 1,000-class subset of it. Do not confuse the size of the full database (about 22,000 categories) with the size of the benchmark (1,000 classes), nor with CIFAR-10's 10 classes.

title: Properties of the multiclass hinge loss
prompt: Which statements about the multiclass hinge loss (SVM loss) are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Incorrect classes whose scores are already below the required margin contribute nothing to the loss
options.explanation: Each wrong class $j$ contributes $\max(0, s_j - s_{y} + \Delta)$. If $s_j \le s_y - \Delta$ the inside is not positive, so the term is clipped to 0.

options.text: It becomes exactly 0 once all margin conditions are satisfied
options.explanation: If the correct score beats every other score by at least the margin, every term in the sum is 0, so the loss is exactly 0. Unlike cross-entropy, it does not keep pushing the scores further apart.

options.text: It uses a margin by which the correct class score must exceed each other class score
options.explanation: The loss is $\sum_{j\ne y}\max(0, s_j - s_y + \Delta)$, so the correct class has to win by at least $\Delta$ against every other class.

options.text: It requires converting the scores to probabilities first
options.explanation: The hinge loss works directly on the raw scores and only compares differences of scores. Converting scores to probabilities with softmax belongs to the cross-entropy loss.

explanation: The multiclass hinge loss $L = \sum_{j\ne y}\max(0, s_j - s_y + \Delta)$ only penalizes classes that violate the margin. Satisfied classes give zero loss and zero gradient, and when all are satisfied the loss is exactly 0. It operates on raw scores, not on probabilities, which is the key practical difference from softmax cross-entropy.

title: Which weight vector does L2 regularization prefer?
prompt: Two weight vectors achieve the same data loss: $w_1 = (1, 1, 0, 0)$ and $w_2 = (2, 0, 0, 0)$. Which one does $L2$ regularization prefer? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Neither; the $L2$ penalty does not depend on the weights
options.explanation: The $L2$ penalty is $\lambda\sum_i w_i^2$, which is a function of the weights; that dependence is exactly how it shrinks them during training.

options.text: Both equally, because the entries of each vector sum to 2
options.explanation: The plain sum (or sum of absolute values, i.e. the $L1$ norm) is indeed 2 for both, but $L2$ squares the entries before summing, which separates the two vectors.

options.text: $w_1$, because its sum of squared entries (2) is smaller than that of $w_2$ (4)
options.explanation: $\sum w_i^2$ is $1+1 = 2$ for $w_1$ and $2^2 = 4$ for $w_2$. The smaller penalty is preferred when the data loss is equal.

options.text: $w_2$, because it has more zero entries
options.explanation: $w_2$ does have more zeros, but $L2$ does not reward sparsity; squaring punishes the single large entry 2 more than two entries of 1. Spreading weight evenly is cheaper under $L2$.

explanation: $L2$ regularization adds $\lambda\sum_i w_i^2$ to the loss. Because the penalty is quadratic, one large weight costs more than the same total magnitude spread across several small weights, so $L2$ prefers the spread-out vector $w_1$ (penalty 2 versus 4). This is why $L2$ gives small, diffuse weights, whereas sparsity is the domain of $L1$.

title: Softmax of three scores
prompt: Applying softmax to the scores $[1.0, 3.0, 0.0]$ gives approximately which probabilities?

options.explanation: $e^{1}\approx 2.718$, $e^{3}\approx 20.086$, $e^{0}=1$ with sum $\approx 23.804$, giving $0.114$, $0.844$ and $0.042$, which round to these values.
These are the right numbers in the wrong order. The largest probability must belong to the largest score, which is the second entry (3.0), not the first (1.0).
A uniform output only occurs when all scores are equal. Here the scores differ, and softmax amplifies differences exponentially.

This treats the scores as if probabilities grew linearly with them. Softmax is exponential: a gap of 2 between the top two scores gives a ratio of $e^{2}\approx 7.4$, not 2, and the lowest score 0.0 still gets about 0.04, not 0.25.

explanation: Softmax is $p_i = \frac{e^{s_i}}{\sum_j e^{s_j}}$. Here the numerators are $2.718$, $20.086$ and $1$, the denominator is $23.804$, so $p \approx [0.114, 0.844, 0.042]$. The probabilities sum to 1, keep the ordering of the scores, and the exponential makes the largest score dominate.

title: Properties of the sigmoid
prompt: Which properties of the sigmoid function $\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$ hold? (Select all that apply)

options.text: sigmoid outputs values in the range $[-1, 1]$
options.explanation: That range belongs to $\tanh$. The sigmoid is never negative: its range is $(0, 1)$.

options.text: $\sigma(x)$ is always strictly between 0 and 1
options.explanation: $e^{-x} > 0$ for every $x$, so the denominator is greater than 1 and $0 < \sigma(x) < 1$. The bounds are approached but never reached.

options.text: sigmoid is monotonically increasing
options.explanation: The derivative is $\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$, which is positive everywhere, so the function always increases (it just becomes very flat for large $|x|$).

options.text: $\sigma(-x) = 1 - \sigma(x)$
options.explanation: $\sigma(-x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{x}} = \frac{e^{-x}}{e^{-x}+1} = 1 - \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$, so the curve is point-symmetric around $(0, 0.5)$.

explanation: The sigmoid squashes any real number into the open interval $(0, 1)$, increases monotonically, equals 0.5 at the origin and satisfies $\sigma(-x) = 1-\sigma(x)$. The usual mix-up is with $\tanh$, which has the range $(-1, 1)$ and is centred at zero. Remember the symmetry and range when interpreting a sigmoid output as a probability.

title: Axis order of an image batch in PyTorch
prompt: In the PyTorch convention, what is the axis order of an image batch tensor (first to last)?

options.text: Height, Width, Channel, Batch
options.explanation: The batch axis comes first, not last. Putting Height, Width, Channel in that order is the layout of a single image in NumPy or PIL, but the batch axis is still at the front.

options.text: Batch, Height, Width, Channel
options.explanation: This 'channels-last' layout (NHWC) is the default in TensorFlow/Keras, not in PyTorch. PyTorch convolutions expect the channel axis directly after the batch axis.

options.text: Channel, Batch, Height, Width
options.explanation: The batch axis is always the first axis in PyTorch, so the channel axis cannot precede it.

options.text: Batch, Channel, Height, Width
options.explanation: This is the NCHW convention: shapes look like $(N, C, H, W)$, e.g. $(N, 3, 32, 32)$ for CIFAR-10.

explanation: PyTorch uses the 'channels-first' layout $(N, C, H, W)$ for image batches, which is what `nn.Conv2d` and `nn.BatchNorm2d` expect. Images loaded with NumPy or PIL are $(H, W, C)$ and must be permuted (`ToTensor` does this) before feeding them into a PyTorch model. Mixing up the two layouts is a very common source of shape errors.

title: Machine learning venues
prompt: Which conferences are primarily machine learning or deep learning venues? (Select all that apply)

options.text: ICRA
options.explanation: ICRA is the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation; it publishes learning-based work, but its focus is robotics.

options.text: ICML
options.explanation: ICML is the International Conference on Machine Learning, one of the main ML venues.

options.text: NeurIPS
options.explanation: NeurIPS (Neural Information Processing Systems) is one of the largest conferences for machine learning and deep learning.

options.text: ICLR
options.explanation: ICLR is the International Conference on Learning Representations, centred on deep learning and representation learning.

options.text: SIGGRAPH
options.explanation: SIGGRAPH is the leading computer graphics and interactive techniques conference. Neural rendering papers appear there, but it is not primarily an ML venue.

explanation: ICML, NeurIPS and ICLR are the flagship machine learning and deep learning conferences, where most new architectures and training methods are published. ICRA (robotics) and SIGGRAPH (graphics) are application-area venues that increasingly feature deep learning, but their main topic is a different field.

title: Sum-of-squares error in polynomial fitting
prompt:
A polynomial $y(x, \mathbf{w}) = w_0 + w_1 x + \dots + w_M x^M$ is fitted to training points $(x_n, t_n)$, $n=1,\dots,N$, by minimizing the sum-of-squares error

$$E(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\big(y(x_n, \mathbf{w}) - t_n\big)^2$$

Assume there are at least $M+1$ distinct inputs $x_n$. Which statements hold? (Select all that apply)

options.text: The error is zero exactly when the fitted curve passes through every training point
options.explanation: $E$ is a sum of squares, so it is 0 only if every residual $y(x_n,\mathbf{w})-t_n$ is 0, i.e. the curve hits every training point.

options.text: The error surface is highly non-convex with many local minima
options.explanation: The polynomial is linear in $\mathbf{w}$, so $E$ is a convex quadratic bowl in the parameters with a single minimum. Non-convex surfaces are a property of deep networks, not of this model.

options.text: The error is a quadratic function of the parameters $\mathbf{w}$
options.explanation: The prediction $y$ is linear in $\mathbf{w}$ (the powers of $x$ are fixed features), and squaring a linear function gives a quadratic function of $\mathbf{w}$.

options.text: A unique global minimum exists and can be found in closed form
options.explanation: Setting the gradient to zero gives the linear normal equations $\Phi^\top\Phi\,\mathbf{w} = \Phi^\top\mathbf{t}$ with solution $\mathbf{w}^* = (\Phi^\top\Phi)^{-1}\Phi^\top\mathbf{t}$, where $\Phi$ is the matrix of powers of the inputs; it is unique when $\Phi$ has full column rank.

explanation: Although the polynomial is non-linear in $x$, it is linear in the parameters $\mathbf{w}$. Therefore the sum-of-squares error is a quadratic, convex function of $\mathbf{w}$: its gradient is linear, there are no spurious local minima, and the unique minimum has a closed-form solution. Zero error means an exact interpolation of the training points, which with a high degree $M$ is possible but leads to overfitting.

title: Can deep learning losses be solved in closed form?
prompt: Can deep learning objectives generally be optimized explicitly (in closed form) with a single global optimum? (Select all that apply)

options.text: No; because such losses cannot be differentiated
options.explanation: Network losses are differentiable (almost everywhere), and backpropagation computes their gradients; this is precisely what makes gradient-based training possible. The obstacle is non-convexity, not a lack of gradients.

options.text: No; they are high-dimensional and non-convex, with many local minima and saddle points
options.explanation: Stacking non-linear layers makes the loss a non-convex function of millions of weights, with local minima and saddle points, so there is no closed-form solution and no guarantee of finding a global optimum.

options.text: Yes; like linear regression they are convex quadratic problems
options.explanation: Linear regression is convex because the model is linear in its parameters. A network composes non-linearities and multiplies weights of different layers, which destroys convexity.

options.text: Yes; provided the learning rate is small enough
options.explanation: The learning rate only controls the step size of an iterative method. It cannot turn a non-convex problem into a convex one or give a closed form; a small step size just converges more stably to some stationary point.

explanation: Least-squares problems such as polynomial fitting have a unique global minimum that can be written down in closed form. Deep network losses are non-convex in the weights, so we rely on iterative, gradient-based methods (SGD and variants) that find good, but not provably global, solutions. Differentiability is what allows this training; non-convexity is what prevents a closed-form answer.

title: Facts about CIFAR-10
prompt: Which statements about the CIFAR-10 dataset are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Each class has 6,000 images
options.explanation: CIFAR-10 has 60,000 images spread evenly over 10 classes, i.e. 6,000 images per class.

options.text: It contains 60,000 color images of size 32x32
options.explanation: The images are small RGB images of 32x32 pixels, 60,000 in total (50,000 train plus 10,000 test).

options.text: The images have a resolution of 224x224
options.explanation: 224x224 is the typical input size for ImageNet models. CIFAR-10 images are only 32x32, which is why they are quick to train on.

options.text: Each image belongs to exactly one of 10 classes
options.explanation: CIFAR-10 is a single-label, 10-class problem (airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, truck).

options.text: It contains 1,000 classes
options.explanation: 1,000 classes is the size of the ILSVRC ImageNet subset. CIFAR-10 has 10 classes (CIFAR-100 has 100).

options.text: 50,000 images are used for training and 10,000 for testing
options.explanation: The standard split is 50,000 training and 10,000 test images (5,000 and 1,000 per class).

explanation: CIFAR-10 consists of 60,000 colour images of 32x32 pixels in 10 balanced classes (6,000 each), split into 50,000 training and 10,000 test images. Its small size makes it a convenient benchmark. Do not confuse it with ImageNet (224x224 inputs, 1,000 classes) or CIFAR-100 (100 classes).

title: Why deep learning took off
prompt: Which factors are commonly cited as reasons deep learning became so effective in recent years? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Deep networks need far less training data than traditional ML methods
options.explanation: It is the opposite: deep networks have many parameters and are data-hungry. Large datasets were a precondition for their success, not something they made unnecessary.

options.text: Availability of very large datasets
options.explanation: Datasets such as ImageNet provide enough labelled examples to train models with millions of parameters without severe overfitting.

options.text: An active community sharing code and ideas (GitHub, arXiv, blogs)
options.explanation: Open sharing of papers, code and pretrained models lets ideas spread and be reproduced and improved very quickly.

options.text: Powerful parallel hardware such as GPUs
options.explanation: Training is dominated by large matrix operations, which GPUs execute in parallel, making large-scale training practical.

options.text: Open-source tools and frameworks such as PyTorch
options.explanation: Frameworks with automatic differentiation and GPU support let researchers build and train new models with little code.

options.text: Deep learning losses are convex, so a global optimum is guaranteed
options.explanation: Deep learning losses are non-convex with many local minima and saddle points. Training works well in practice, but no global optimum is guaranteed.

explanation: The recent success of deep learning is usually attributed to the combination of big data, parallel compute (GPUs), open-source software and an open research community. It does not come from reduced data needs or from an easy optimization problem: deep nets need lots of data, and their loss is non-convex.

title: Facts about CIFAR-100
prompt: Which statements about the CIFAR-100 dataset are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Each class has 500 training images and 100 test images
options.explanation: Each of the 100 classes has 600 images, split into 500 for training and 100 for testing.

options.text: It has more images per class than CIFAR-10
options.explanation: CIFAR-100 has only 600 images per class, whereas CIFAR-10 has 6,000. Both datasets have the same total size, so more classes means fewer images per class.

options.text: The 100 classes are grouped into 20 superclasses
options.explanation: CIFAR-100 has a two-level hierarchy: 20 coarse superclasses (e.g. vehicles, flowers), each containing 5 fine classes.

options.text: It contains 100,000 images in total
options.explanation: The total is $100 \times 600 = 60{,}000$ images, the same as CIFAR-10. The number 100 refers to the classes, not the images.

options.text: It has 100 classes with 600 images per class
options.explanation: 100 classes with 600 images each give 60,000 images, of which 50,000 are for training and 10,000 for testing.

explanation: CIFAR-100 has the same 60,000 images of 32x32 pixels as CIFAR-10, but divided into 100 classes of 600 images (500 train and 100 test), which are grouped into 20 superclasses. With 10 times fewer examples per class it is a harder problem than CIFAR-10. Compute totals from the per-class numbers to avoid confusing the number of classes with the number of images.

title: Averaging the loss over a batch
prompt: Why is the loss usually averaged (rather than summed) over the samples of a batch? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Averaging guarantees a convex loss
options.explanation: Convexity depends on the model and the loss function, not on how per-sample losses are combined. Dividing by a constant $N$ does not change the shape of the loss surface.

options.text: Averaging removes the need for a learning rate
options.explanation: The gradient of the average still has to be scaled by a step size. Averaging only makes the good learning rate less dependent on the batch size.

options.text: The loss scale becomes independent of the batch size, which stabilizes gradient magnitudes
options.explanation: A sum grows proportionally with the batch size $N$, and so does its gradient, whereas the mean stays on the same scale. A learning rate tuned for one batch size then still works reasonably for another.

options.text: Summing would make the loss negative
options.explanation: Common losses (cross-entropy, squared error, hinge) are non-negative per sample, so their sum is non-negative as well. The sign is not affected.

explanation: The mean and the sum differ only by the constant factor $N$, so they have the same minimizer, but the gradient of the sum scales with the batch size. Averaging keeps the loss and gradient magnitudes comparable across batch sizes (and for a smaller last batch), which makes the learning rate easier to choose. It has no effect on convexity, the sign of the loss, or the need for a learning rate.

title: Traditional ML versus deep learning
prompt: Which statements correctly contrast traditional machine learning with deep learning? (Select all that apply)

options.text: In traditional ML, the feature extractor and the classifier are usually trained jointly end to end
options.explanation: In a traditional pipeline the feature extractor is designed by hand and fixed, and only the classifier is trained on top of it. Joint end-to-end training is the hallmark of deep learning.

options.text: Deep networks typically have far more trainable parameters and can exploit much larger datasets than traditional ML pipelines
options.explanation: Deep networks have millions of parameters and keep improving with more data, whereas classical pipelines with few parameters tend to saturate.

options.text: Traditional ML often relies on handcrafted, problem-specific features, while deep learning learns feature representations from data
options.explanation: Examples of handcrafted features are SIFT or HOG, designed by experts for a task. Deep networks learn their features in the hidden layers directly from the data.

options.text: In deep learning, feature extraction and classification are trained jointly within one network
options.explanation: The early layers act as feature extractor and the last layer as classifier, and backpropagation trains all of them together on one loss.

options.text: Deep learning generally requires fewer training samples than traditional ML
options.explanation: Because deep networks have so many parameters and learn features from scratch, they generally need more data than traditional methods that use strong handcrafted priors.

explanation: Traditional ML splits the problem into hand-engineered feature extraction and a separately trained classifier. Deep learning merges both in one network trained end to end, so the features are learned. The price is a much larger number of parameters and a greater need for data and compute, not a smaller one.

title: Recognizing unsupervised learning tasks
prompt: Which of the following are typical examples of unsupervised learning? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Training a spam filter on messages marked as spam or not spam
options.explanation: The messages come with spam/not-spam labels, so this is supervised classification.

options.text: Classifying images using human-provided class labels
options.explanation: Human-provided class labels are exactly the supervision that defines supervised learning.

options.text: Detecting anomalies without any labeled anomalies
options.explanation: Without labelled anomalies the model learns what normal data looks like (e.g. a density or a reconstruction) and flags points that deviate, which needs no labels.

options.text: Reducing data dimensionality with PCA
options.explanation: PCA finds directions of maximum variance using only the inputs, without any target values.

options.text: Clustering customers by purchasing behavior
options.explanation: Clustering groups similar samples based on their features alone; there are no predefined group labels.

explanation: Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data: clustering, dimensionality reduction (PCA) and anomaly detection without labelled anomalies are classic examples. As soon as a task has human-provided labels for each sample (spam filter, image classification), it is supervised. The test is simply whether the training data contains target labels.

title: Scale variation as an image classification challenge
prompt: In the list of image classification challenges (viewpoint, illumination, occlusion, ...), 'scale variation' refers primarily to: (Select all that apply)

options.text: Differences in the number of images per class
options.explanation: That is class imbalance, a dataset property. Scale variation is about how objects look, not about how many examples exist.

options.text: Variation in the number of pixels across image files
options.explanation: Different file resolutions are a data preparation issue that is fixed by resizing. Scale variation remains even when all images have the same resolution.

options.text: Variation in the real-world size of objects, not only their extent in the image
options.explanation: Instances of one class can differ in real size (e.g. small and large dogs) and appear larger or smaller in the image depending on distance, so the classifier must cope with objects at many scales.

options.text: Rescaling pixel intensities to the range [0, 1]
options.explanation: Intensity rescaling is a normalization step in preprocessing. It changes brightness values, not the size of objects.

explanation: Scale variation is one of the intrinsic difficulties of recognizing objects: members of the same category come in different physical sizes and appear at different sizes in the image. A good classifier has to recognize them regardless. Class imbalance, image file size and intensity normalization are separate issues.

title: Defining self-supervised learning
prompt: Which statements best describe self-supervised learning? (Select all that apply)

options.text: No external labels are given; supervision signals are generated from the data itself, e.g., predicting future video frames
options.explanation: Self-supervised learning creates a prediction task from the data (predict a future frame, a masked word, a missing patch), so the target comes for free without human annotation.

options.text: Learning is driven by a scalar reward from a dynamic environment
options.explanation: This is reinforcement learning, where an agent learns from rewards obtained by acting in an environment.

options.text: A small labeled subset is combined with a large unlabeled set
options.explanation: This is semi-supervised learning. It still uses human-provided labels for a part of the data, whereas self-supervised learning needs none.

options.text: Every training sample has a human-provided label
options.explanation: This is plain supervised learning. Self-supervised methods do not rely on human annotations.

explanation: Self-supervised learning builds its own labels from the structure of the data, for example by hiding part of the input and predicting it from the rest. It therefore uses a supervised-style loss without human annotation. Distinguish it from supervised (human labels), semi-supervised (some labels) and reinforcement learning (rewards).

title: Closed-form fit versus deep network training
prompt: Fitting a polynomial with a sum-of-squares error can be solved in closed form with a guaranteed global optimum, but training a deep neural network cannot. Explain why, and say how deep networks are trained instead.
model_answer: The polynomial is linear in its parameters, so the sum-of-squares error is a convex quadratic in them: setting its gradient to zero gives linear equations with a unique solution. A deep network composes many non-linear layers, so its loss is a non-convex function of millions of weights with many local minima and saddle points, and no closed-form solution exists. Because the loss is still differentiable, networks are trained iteratively with gradient descent variants (SGD), which find good solutions but give no global-optimum guarantee.
key_points: The polynomial model is linear in its parameters, so the squared error is a convex quadratic with a unique minimum.
Setting the gradient to zero gives linear (normal) equations that can be solved directly.
Deep network losses are non-convex in the weights, with many local minima and saddle points, so there is no closed form or global guarantee.
Networks are trained iteratively with gradient-based optimization (backpropagation plus SGD) because the loss is differentiable.
hints: Which quantity must be linear for the squared error to be quadratic: the input x or the parameters w?
What happens to convexity when you stack non-linear layers?
explanation: The key distinction is linearity in the parameters, not in the input: a polynomial is non-linear in x but linear in w, so least squares is a convex bowl. A neural network is non-linear in its weights, which makes the landscape non-convex. Frequent half-answers: saying that deep losses 'cannot be differentiated' (they can, which is why gradient descent works) or that a small learning rate would fix the problem (it only affects stability of the iterative method).

title: Where the training signal comes from
prompt: Compare supervised, unsupervised and self-supervised learning in terms of where the training signal comes from. Why is self-supervised learning not simply a kind of supervised learning with human labels?
model_answer: In supervised learning every input comes with a human-provided label and the model learns a mapping from inputs to labels. In unsupervised learning there are no targets at all and the model looks for structure such as clusters, low-dimensional representations or anomalies. In self-supervised learning there are also no external labels, but the labels are generated from the data itself (for example, predicting a masked part or a future video frame from the rest), so training looks like supervised learning while needing no human annotation.
key_points: Supervised learning uses externally provided (human) labels for each input.
Unsupervised learning has no targets and finds structure such as clusters, PCA directions or anomalies.
Self-supervised learning creates its own labels from the data, e.g. by predicting a missing or future part of the input.
Self-supervised needs no human annotation, which allows learning from very large unlabeled datasets.
hints: For each paradigm, ask: who or what provides the target value?
Think of predicting the next video frame from the previous ones.
explanation: The distinguishing question is the origin of the supervision signal: external annotation (supervised), none (unsupervised), or the data itself (self-supervised). A common half-answer is to call self-supervised learning 'unsupervised' because no human labels exist; but it does optimize a prediction loss against automatically built targets. Another is to confuse it with semi-supervised learning, which still needs some human labels.

title: Input and output of image classification
prompt: Which choices correctly describe the input and output of the image classification problem? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Input: an RGB image; Output: a label for every pixel of the image
options.explanation: A label for every pixel is semantic segmentation. Image classification assigns a single prediction to the whole image, not one per pixel.

options.text: Input: a text prompt and noise; Output: an RGB image
options.explanation: This describes a text-to-image generative model (for example a diffusion model). Classification maps an image to a class prediction, not the other way round.

options.text: Input: an RGB image; Output: a vector of class probabilities with one entry per class
options.explanation: A classifier maps an image to K scores, typically turned into probabilities with softmax, one per class. The predicted class is the entry with the highest probability.

options.text: Input: an RGB image; Output: a list of bounding boxes with class labels
options.explanation: Boxes with labels are the output of object detection, which also has to localise objects. Classification only says what the image contains as a whole.

hints: Ask yourself how many predictions the task produces per image.
Segmentation, detection and generation are different tasks with different outputs.
explanation: Image classification maps one image to one distribution over a fixed set of classes. Tasks that look similar differ in the output: segmentation gives one label per pixel, detection gives boxes plus labels, and text-to-image generation reverses the direction by producing an image. Always identify the task by what is predicted per input.

title: Which categories appear in CIFAR-10
prompt: Which of the following are CIFAR-10 classes? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Ship
options.explanation: Ship is one of the ten CIFAR-10 classes (airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, truck).

options.text: Flower
options.explanation: CIFAR-10 contains only vehicles and animals. Flowers appear in other datasets (and in CIFAR-100 as a superclass), which is the likely source of confusion.

options.text: Person
options.explanation: There is no person class in CIFAR-10; its classes are 6 animals and 4 vehicle types. Person is a class in detection datasets such as COCO.

options.text: Frog
options.explanation: Frog is one of the six animal classes of CIFAR-10.

options.text: Deer
options.explanation: Deer is one of the six animal classes of CIFAR-10.

options.text: Airplane
options.explanation: Airplane is one of the four vehicle classes of CIFAR-10, together with automobile, ship and truck.

hints: CIFAR-10 has ten classes: six animals and four vehicles.
Think of 32x32 colour images of everyday animals and vehicles.
explanation: CIFAR-10 consists of 60,000 colour images of size 32x32 in ten mutually exclusive classes: airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship and truck. Flowers and people are not among them. Knowing the dataset's classes (10 outputs, 32x32x3 inputs) helps you size the final layer of a classifier.

title: Traditional machine learning versus deep learning
prompt: Which of the following are traditional machine learning tools rather than deep learning architectures? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Decision trees
options.explanation: Decision trees split the feature space with learned thresholds. They are a classical model with no layered neural representation.

options.text: k-nearest neighbors (kNN)
options.explanation: kNN classifies a point by the labels of its closest training samples. It has no trained network and is a classical, non-parametric method.

options.text: Principal component analysis (PCA)
options.explanation: PCA is a classical linear dimensionality reduction method based on the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (or the SVD).

options.text: Generative adversarial networks (GANs)
options.explanation: A GAN consists of two neural networks, a generator and a discriminator, trained against each other. It is a deep learning architecture.

options.text: Support vector machines (SVM)
options.explanation: SVMs find a maximum-margin separator, possibly with a kernel. They are a classical method that does not learn layered features.

options.text: Transformer architectures
options.explanation: Transformers are deep neural networks built from attention and feed-forward layers, so they belong to deep learning.

hints: Deep learning architectures are neural networks with several learned layers.
Which of these have no neural network in them at all?
explanation: Decision trees, kNN, PCA and SVMs were developed before the deep learning era and do not learn hierarchical features through stacked neural layers. GANs and Transformers are neural architectures trained with gradient descent. The distinction is whether the model is a (deep) neural network, not whether it is accurate or popular.

title: Result shape of a broadcast addition
prompt: Using broadcasting, adding a tensor of shape (4, 3) and a tensor of shape (3,) produces a result of which shape?

options.explanation: Shapes are aligned from the right: 3 matches 3, and the missing leading dimension of the vector is treated as 1 and stretched to 4. The result has shape (4, 3).

options.text: It raises an error
options.explanation: Broadcasting is allowed because the trailing dimensions are equal (3 and 3). An error would only occur if two aligned dimensions differed and neither was 1.
The result has the larger of the two shapes along each dimension, so it cannot lose the dimension of size 3. Reducing over the last axis would need an explicit sum.
Broadcasting never permutes dimensions. The first tensor already has shape (4, 3), so the result keeps that order.

hints: Align the shapes starting from the last (rightmost) dimension.
A missing leading dimension behaves like a dimension of size 1.
explanation: Broadcasting aligns shapes from the right, and two dimensions are compatible if they are equal or one of them is 1 (or missing). Here (4, 3) and (3,) become (4, 3) and (1, 3), and the vector is repeated across the 4 rows. This is exactly how a bias vector of size K is added to a batch of outputs of shape (N, K).

title: Per-sample dot products of two batches
prompt: $X$ and $Y$ are tensors of shape $(N,D)$. Which lines compute the per-sample dot products as a vector of shape $(N,)$? (Select all that apply)

options.text: `torch.dot(X, Y)`
options.explanation: `torch.dot` only accepts two 1-D tensors of the same length and raises an error for 2-D inputs. It does not work row by row.

options.text: `(X * Y).sum(dim=0)`
options.explanation: The element-wise product has shape (N, D), but summing over dim=0 adds up the samples and returns a vector of shape (D,). That is a per-feature sum, not a per-sample dot product.
This computes all N x N pairwise dot products, a matrix of shape (N, N). Only its diagonal contains the per-sample dot products, so the result is not an (N,) vector.

options.text: `(X * Y).sum(dim=1)`
options.explanation: The element-wise product multiplies matching features, and summing over the feature axis (dim=1) leaves one dot product per sample, shape (N,).

options.text: `torch.einsum('nd,nd->n', X, Y)`
options.explanation: The index d appears in both inputs but not in the output, so it is multiplied and summed; n is kept. The output has shape (N,).

hints: Which axis holds the features that must be summed, and which holds the samples that must be kept?
Write down the output shape of each candidate line.
explanation: A per-sample dot product multiplies matching features and sums over the feature axis only: $z_n = \sum_d X_{nd} Y_{nd}$. That is `(X * Y).sum(dim=1)` or the einsum `nd,nd->n`. Summing over the wrong axis gives shape (D,), a full matrix product gives (N, N), and `torch.dot` is restricted to 1-D vectors. Checking output shapes is the fastest way to rule out candidates.

title: Shapes of weights and bias in a linear classifier
prompt: A linear classifier computes $y=Wx+b$ for an input $x\in \mathbb{R}^{D}$ and $K$ classes. Which statements about the shapes are correct? (Select all that apply)

options.text: $W$ is a $D\times K$ matrix and $b$ is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{D}$
options.explanation: A $D\times K$ matrix cannot multiply a column vector $x\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ as $Wx$ (it would need $x^\top W$), and the bias must have one entry per output, i.e. $K$, not $D$.

options.text: $W$ is a $D\times D$ matrix and $b$ is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{K}$
options.explanation: With a $D\times D$ matrix, $Wx$ has $D$ entries, so it cannot be added to a bias with $K$ entries (unless $D=K$) and does not yield $K$ class scores.

options.text: $W$ is a $K\times K$ matrix and $b$ is a scalar
options.explanation: A $K\times K$ matrix does not match an input of size $D$ in general, and a single scalar bias would force all classes to share the same offset instead of one learnable offset per class.

options.text: $W$ is a $K\times D$ matrix and $b$ is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{K}$
options.explanation: Each of the $K$ rows of $W$ is a template of length $D$, so $Wx\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$, and the bias has one entry per class, $b\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$.

hints: The output $y$ must have one score per class.
For $Wx$ to be defined, the number of columns of $W$ must equal the length of $x$.
explanation: For $y=Wx+b$ with $x\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ and $y\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$, the matrix must map $D$ inputs to $K$ outputs, so $W\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$. The layer has $KD+K$ trainable parameters. Reading the shape off 'columns = input size, rows = output size' avoids most mix-ups; note that PyTorch stores `nn.Linear` weights as (out_features, in_features) for exactly this reason.

title: What characterises reinforcement learning
prompt: Which statements best describe reinforcement learning? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Missing parts of the input are predicted from observed parts
options.explanation: Predicting masked or missing parts of the data from the rest is self-supervised learning (as in masked autoencoders or language modelling), not reinforcement learning.

options.text: An agent interacts with a dynamic environment and learns to maximize a reward
options.explanation: This is the definition of reinforcement learning: an agent takes actions, the environment responds with new states and rewards, and the agent learns a policy that maximises the cumulative reward.

options.text: A mapping is learned from a fixed set of labeled examples
options.explanation: Learning from a fixed set of input-label pairs is supervised learning. Reinforcement learning has no fixed labelled dataset, only reward feedback from interaction.

options.text: Clusters are found in unlabeled data
options.explanation: Finding structure such as clusters in data without labels is unsupervised learning. Reinforcement learning is driven by reward, not by data structure.

hints: Which paradigm involves actions and rewards?
Match each statement with supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised or reinforcement learning.
explanation: The learning paradigms differ in the feedback they use: labels (supervised), no feedback beyond the data structure (unsupervised), parts of the data itself (self-supervised), and a reward signal from interaction with an environment (reinforcement learning). The agent's actions influence what data it sees next, which is what makes reinforcement learning different from learning on a fixed dataset.

title: Hyperparameters versus trainable parameters
